ai_summary: Great Britain is currently generating a total wind output of 10.3 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output delivering 3.8 GW, which represents 37.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Scotland currently demonstrates the deep decarbonisation potential of renewables with a local carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in stark contrast to the GB-wide carbon intensity of 69 gCO2/kWh. However, persistent north-to-south transmission boundary limitations continue to stifle this clean generation. Due to network bottlenecks, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 37.3 GWh through Balancing Mechanism bid actions, incurring a constraint cost of about £2,338,976. Because clean northern energy cannot flow freely to demand centres, system operators have been forced to fire up thermal generation south of the constraint boundary. Consequently, an estimated 7,093,574 m3 of gas was burned elsewhere to replace this lost output, driving 13,067 tonnes of CO2 emissions that could have been avoided. Annualised across a full year, this level of constraint yields an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of £854 million, adding an estimated £3/MWh to UK consumer electricity invoices and highlighting the urgent economic imperative for strategic transmission network expansion.
